newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Trygg-Hansa expects Home to pay interest.
newsitem.headline: Trygg-Hansa expects Home to pay interest.

text.p: Swedish insurer Trygg-Hansa AB said on Tuesday it expects its troubled former subsidiary, Home Holdings of the U.S., to pay interest on loans from Trygg-Hansa in mid-July.
Trygg-Hansa said on Monday that Home Holdings cannot pay interest due on June 15 but that the group has a 30 day respite before the loans fall due.
In total, Home Holdings loans amount to $280 million, of which Trygg-Hansa holds a part. Home Holdings is due to pay a total of $11.6 million in interest every six months.
Trygg-Hansa has previously estimated that its link to the U.S. group has cost it around four billion crowns. It now risks losing another 354 million crowns worth of loans and shares.

Jan Bruneheim, a Trygg-Hansa executive who is also a director of Home Holdings said the non-payment allows Home a stronger hand in negotiations with policyholders about buying back policies, with its landlord about lower rent and smaller office space and with owners of a bond loan,
"Home Insurance is taking part in three large negotiations at the moment and the weaker result and balance sheet it has, the stronger its negotiating position is," he said.
Home Holdings has no assets of its own and is dependent on dividends from Home Insurance to be able to pay interest.

If Home Holdings is unable to pay interest, the U.S. insurance authority New Hampshire Insurance Department, whose task it is to safeguard policyholders, will take over the handling of Home Insurance's affairs, he said.

"The parties now negotiating with Home Insurance know that they have a month to reach a solution, then they must start negotiating with a new party who will look after policy holders," Bruneheim said.
Therefore negotiations with the landlord and bond holders should be finalised during this time period, Bruneheim said.
If Home Insurance succeeds with this plan it can then pay dividends to Home Holdings which in turn can pay its interest charges.
"This is the scenario you must assume at the moment," Bruneheim said.
